Koch's Snowflake

LimitsSequencesArea
Game: Start with a triangle and keep putting a small triangular tent on the middle of every side. See how long the outline gets while the shape hardly grows.
How to play: Move the slider to do more rounds. Read the number of sides, the length of the outline and the area underneath.

Look for the math

If a sequence of curves closes in on a limit curve, do their lengths close in on the length of the limit? Not always. Here every curve has a finite length, but the lengths grow without bound, so the limit curve has no finite length at all, although it fits inside a circle.

Counting segments and length

Start with the triangle: 3 segments of length 1 (side 1), total 3. Each step cuts every segment into three parts and replaces the middle one by two sides of a tent, so each segment becomes 4 segments a third as long. After n steps (the slider shows N = n + 1) there are 3 · 4n segments of length 1/3n, and the total is 3 (4/3)n: 3, 4, 16/3, 64/9, and so on. Since 4/3 > 1, this is a geometric progression with no upper bound. The test measured the real outline for every N up to 8 and found exactly these numbers.

But the shape stays small

Every point of every curve lies inside the circle through the corners of the starting triangle (the dashed circle). And the area converges: each step adds a ring of small triangles, and the sum comes to 8/5 of the starting triangle, exactly 8/5 − (3/5)(4/9)n after n steps. The test checked this against the measured area of the drawn outline. So the Koch snowflake has a finite area but an infinite perimeter.

Move the slider to the end and look at the table: the length column keeps growing by a third each row, while the area column hardly moves.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
